sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Define (i) motivation; (ii) need.
questions.answer: (i) The process of being moved towards a goal by wants, needs or motives. (ii) A lack of something necessary for us.

questions.q: Name any two primary needs.
questions.answer: Hunger, thirst, oxygen, rest, sleep, temperature regulation, shelter (any two).

questions.q: Differentiate intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in one line each.
questions.answer: Intrinsic motivation comes from within, from enjoyment of the task; extrinsic motivation is based on external rewards such as money and grades.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) Emotions prepare us for action. (ii) When we feel an emotion no bodily changes take place.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) False.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) Emotional expression is shown only through the face. (ii) Labelling of emotions is influenced by past experience and culture.
questions.answer: (i) False – also posture and gestures. (ii) True.

questions.q: Name any two social motives.
questions.answer: Achievement, affiliation, power, nurturance, aggression, exploration (any two).

questions.q: Name the three types of needs other than primary and secondary classification.
questions.answer: Existence needs, relatedness needs and growth needs.

questions.q: Name the six primary emotions seen in facial expression.
questions.answer: Fear, anger, sadness, surprise, disgust and happiness.

questions.q: What is homeostasis?
questions.answer: The body's state of balance in water, temperature and glucose levels.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has four parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Identify the social motive: (i) seeking company of others; (ii) influencing others; (iii) fighting to overcome opposition; (iv) seeking novelty.
questions.answer: (i) Affiliation. (ii) Power. (iii) Aggression. (iv) Exploration.

questions.q: Name the component of emotion: (i) increased heart rate; (ii) smiling and frowning; (iii) labelling the feeling as 'happy'; (iv) the part which is the most important in emotional experience.
questions.answer: (i) Physiological changes. (ii) Behavioural changes/expression. (iii) Emotional feelings. (iv) Cognition (understanding of the situation).

questions.q: Name the environmental factor affecting hunger: (i) liking for pizza; (ii) eating more under exam pressure; (iii) feeling hungry at dinner time; (iv) craving sweets after the doctor's ban.
questions.answer: (i) Learned liking and habits. (ii) Stress. (iii) External cues. (iv) Dietary restraints.

questions.q: Arrange in Maslow's order from the base: safety, self-actualisation, biological, esteem.
questions.answer: Biological, safety, esteem, self-actualisation.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Differentiate primary and secondary motives.
questions.answer: Primary motives are biological and due to physiological imbalance (hunger, thirst); secondary motives are psychological or social and learnt through social experience (achievement, affiliation).

questions.q: What is self-actualisation?
questions.answer: The highest need in Maslow's hierarchy: reaching one's full potential, being self-aware, socially responsive and open to the challenges of life.

questions.q: Why is optimum arousal necessary for motivation?
questions.answer: Too little arousal makes us dull and relaxed, too much makes us withdraw from the goal, so a balanced level keeps us motivated.

questions.q: Why do we feel thirsty?
questions.answer: Because the body loses water through perspiration, breathing and urination.

questions.q: What are display rules?
questions.answer: Culturally approved ways of expressing emotion, learnt in childhood, e.g. Japanese show less emotional display than Italians.

questions.q: Give one function of emotions.
questions.answer: They prepare us for action, e.g. fear helps us to run away from danger.

questions.q: How can an emotion act as a motive?
questions.answer: A frightened child cries out for help and seeks comfort and security from a parent.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the characteristics of motivation.
questions.answer: Motivation pushes us to goals and needs optimum arousal; it is influenced by pleasing external stimuli such as money and food; it results from thoughts and expectations and may be intrinsic or extrinsic; and needs are ordered, basic needs first.

questions.q: Describe the factors in the hunger need.
questions.answer: Stomach contractions and low blood glucose and protein cause hunger; smell, taste and look of food add to it; environment matters through learned liking, stress, external cues and dietary restraints.

questions.q: Describe the social motives.
questions.answer: Social motives are learned in groups, mainly the family: achievement, affiliation, power, nurturance, aggression and exploration; their strength differs from person to person.

questions.q: Explain the functions of emotions.
questions.answer: Emotions prepare us for action, help arrange activities and future behaviour (positive emotions reinforce), and help us interact effectively with others by showing how we are likely to act.

questions.q: Explain the components of emotion with an example.
questions.answer: Physiological changes (heart rate, perspiration before an exam), behavioural expression (facial expressions, gestures) and subjective feelings labelled by experience and culture.

questions.q: How does culture influence emotion?
questions.answer: The six basic emotions are expressed universally, but cultures differ in display rules learnt through childhood experiences; people may also mask emotions, as with a polite smile at an unwanted gift.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
questions.answer: Maslow ranked needs from biological at the base, then safety, belongingness and love, self-esteem, cognitive needs, aesthetic needs, and self-actualisation at the top. Lower needs are met first, but a person may move up and down the hierarchy and cultures differ (Sweden and Norway value social needs; some cultures value job security over satisfaction).

questions.q: Discuss primary and secondary needs with examples and environmental influences.
questions.answer: Primary needs (hunger, thirst, oxygen, sleep, warmth) arise from physiological imbalance and homeostasis; hunger is influenced by learned liking, stress, external cues and dietary restraints. Secondary needs (achievement, affiliation, power, nurturance, aggression, exploration) are learned socially, e.g. Mother Teresa high on nurturance and Mandela on achievement.

questions.q: What are emotions? Explain their functions and components.
questions.answer: Emotions are strong feelings from pleasant or unpleasant experiences. They prepare us for action, organise future behaviour, and help interaction. Components: physiological changes, behavioural expression (six primary facial emotions) and feelings; cognition is essential, and culture shapes display rules.

questions.q: Discuss the role of motivation and emotion in organising behaviour.
questions.answer: Both activate, control and plan behaviour. Motivation is accompanied by emotions (success brings joy and pride) and emotions motivate us to repeat or avoid situations. Emotions can serve as motives (a frightened child seeks comfort); without them we would act in a robotic fashion.
